title: Incentive Super-Response Tendency
hook: Show people the prize, and the room starts noticing different facts.
coreIdea: Incentive super-response tendency is the way rewards and penalties can pull attention, belief, and behavior harder than people admit.
counterintuition: The first question is not whether someone is good or bad. It is what the system is paying them to see, ignore, defend, hurry, or call success.
tryThisNow: Before judging a strange behavior, write the reward beside it. Ask what the person gains by repeating that behavior.
keyTakeaway: Inspect the incentive before you moralize the response.

breakdown.fastRead:
A lab notebook sits open in the wildfire planning room while Ronan reviews fuel-clearing proposals. The contractor with the biggest acreage bonus keeps recommending larger cuts. The map may be right. The reward is still pulling on it.

Incentives change attention. They tell people what to count, what to defend, and what to call progress. Once the payoff is clear, behavior can move farther and faster than polite explanations suggest.

The reward points the eyes.

The correction is to mark the incentive in the room, then ask what behavior it makes easy, tempting, or invisible before accepting the recommendation.
breakdown.deepRead:
The lab notebook in Ronan's wildfire office lists slope, wind, tree density, and last year's burns. The contractor's proposal sounds technical, but the payment rule pays by cleared hectare. Ronan writes incentives beside the notebook and asks the team to score risk reduction per hectare, not hectares cleared.

Incentives do not make people machines. They do something subtler. They bend the search. A person paid for volume finds volume. A person rewarded for speed notices speed. A person punished for bad news delays bad news. The incentive does not have to be secret or corrupt. It only has to be strong enough to become the path of least resistance.

Follow the payoff before judging the speech.

A good review asks what the system rewards, what it punishes, and what it leaves unmeasured. If salespeople are paid for contracts signed, they may stop noticing whether the customer can succeed. If doctors are paid by procedure, procedure may look more natural. If a software team is praised for sign-ups, it may treat retention as someone else's problem.

A software beta dashboard shows this cleanly. Saskia is reading a contract redline after the vendor promises a flood of beta users. The bonus pays for activated accounts, not useful feedback. She writes super-response on the redline and changes the contract to pay for completed test tasks and bug reports instead.

Design the reward for the behavior you actually want.
breakdown.fullRead:
A biotech signal review room smells of cold coffee and marker ink. Irene has a menu proof from the investor lunch beside the trial summary because the company is preparing a fundraising event. The scientists want to highlight a borderline subgroup result. The subgroup may matter. The financing deadline also matters. Irene writes fish lures on the menu proof.

Fish lures are made for the fish, not the angler. Incentives work the same way. The reward does not care what people say they value; it pulls on what the system has made worth catching. That is why incentives can change not only behavior, but belief. People begin to notice the facts that help the payoff and discount the facts that threaten it.

Charlie Munger treated incentive super-response as one of the strongest forces in human judgment because it can override good intentions while leaving everyone with a reasonable-sounding explanation. The lesson is not that character is fake. It is that character works inside a current of rewards and penalties.

Who gets paid, praised, protected, or punished if this answer wins?

Irene uses that question on the biotech signal. The subgroup result goes into the appendix with its sample size and uncertainty. The main deck leads with the primary endpoint. If the subgroup is real, it can survive further testing. If it is only a fundraising lure, the revised deck removes the reward for overstating it.

You can feel the same pull in a cycling crash audit. You are holding a case file after a courier company rewards riders for deliveries per hour. Pablo, the safety lead, sees managers blaming reckless cyclists. He marks reward design on the file and must choose: discipline riders alone or change the pay rule that rewards speed through dangerous intersections.

This is not an excuse for bad conduct. It is a map of pressure.

People still make choices. Ethics still matter. But a system that pays for the wrong thing should not be surprised when it gets a super-response to the wrong thing. The clearest fix is often not a speech about values. It is a better incentive, a countermeasure, or a guardrail that makes the desired behavior worth doing.

So look at incentives early. Look before the scandal, before the missed safety signal, before the sales spike that will later become refunds. Ask what the reward makes visible and what it hides. If the answer points away from the stated goal, redesign the reward before the reward redesigns the people.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Incentives can bend attention and behavior before anyone admits they are being pulled. Readers need to inspect payoff design before judging conduct or trusting recommendations.

examples.title: Ronan Changes the Fire Metric

planSpec.domain: a wildfire planning room applying Incentive Super-Response Tendency under operational pressure
planSpec.audience: a reader who has to make a live judgment where incentives could mislead them
planSpec.stakes: public safety and budgets get misallocated if incentive super-response is treated as a slogan

examples.scenario: The wildfire planning room smells of pine dust at 8:15 a.m. while Ronan opens a lab notebook beside three fuel-clearing maps. The contractor paid by hectare recommends the widest cut. Before approving the plan, Ronan must decide whether acreage is steering the advice, so he writes incentives in the notebook.
examples.whatToDo: Score risk reduction per hectare and cap payment on measured hazard reduction, not raw area cleared.
examples.whyItMatters: The contractor may be competent, but the reward points toward more hectares. The plan should pay for reduced fire risk, not visible activity.

examples.title: Saskia Rewrites the Beta Bonus

planSpec.domain: a software beta dashboard applying Incentive Super-Response Tendency under operational pressure
planSpec.audience: a reader who has to make a live judgment where super-response could mislead them
planSpec.stakes: product quality and customer trust get misallocated if incentive super-response is treated as a slogan

examples.scenario: "We can bring five thousand beta users," the vendor says as Saskia reads the contract redline beside the dashboard. The bonus pays for activated accounts. It says nothing about completed tasks or useful bug reports. Saskia weighs whether to buy sign-ups or redesign the reward, so she writes super-response on the redline. At the handoff, Saskia has to pause the tidy story and test the record. Before the contract moves, Saskia must decide whether to buy sign-ups or redesign the reward around completed useful work.
examples.whatToDo: Tie payment to completed test tasks, verified bug reports, and retention after onboarding. Do not pay only for accounts created.
examples.whyItMatters: A sign-up bonus will produce sign-ups. If the goal is learning, the incentive has to pay for learning behavior.

examples.scenario: It took Adele one sensor graph from the stage-rigging team to see why every touring budget looked optimistic. Producers earned bonuses when the tour was approved, not when load-in times were accurate. Adele writes Munger risk on the graph and decides whether to accept the rosy budget or attach bonuses to actual tour variance. With the file still open, Adele faces a choice: act on the claim now or check the missing evidence first.
examples.whatToDo: Tie producer bonuses to budget accuracy and safe load-in estimates, not approval alone. Require variance tracking before the next green light.
examples.whyItMatters: The optimistic budget is not just optimism. The reward makes approval attractive and accuracy optional.

examples.whyItMatters: The adviser may believe the product is good, but the fee design pulls attention toward complexity. The committee needs to see that pull.

reviewCards.front: A behavior looks strange or harmful. What should you inspect first?
reviewCards.back: Inspect the reward or penalty attached to it. The incentive may be pulling attention and behavior.

reviewCards.front: Why is moralizing too early risky?
reviewCards.back: It can miss the system that pays for the conduct. Better reward design may prevent repetition.
A strong behavioral reaction to a reward, often stronger than people admit or notice.

reviewCards.front: A metric improves while the real goal worsens. What likely happened?
reviewCards.back: The incentive rewarded the metric, so people optimized it while ignoring the unmeasured goal.

reviewCards.front: How do you redesign a bad incentive?
reviewCards.back: Pay for the behavior and outcome you actually want, then add guardrails for what the reward might hide.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to find the reward behind a behavior and redesign the incentive before blaming character or trusting recommendations.

ifThenPlans.plan: If behavior seems irrational or unethical, then I will write what the person is paid, praised, or punished for before judging.
If a vendor promises volume, then I will check whether payment rewards volume, quality, retention, or real learning.
If one metric improves while the goal worsens, then I will inspect whether the incentive rewards the metric alone.
If an adviser recommends a product, then I will ask how they are compensated before weighing the recommendation.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, pick one recurring behavior that frustrates you. Write the reward beside it and name one better incentive.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, audit one metric or bonus system for the behavior it may overproduce and the outcome it may hide.
